name: Safavid Iran
title: Social Hierarchy of Safavid Iran: From Shah to Enslaved

tiers.name: The shah
tiers.you: Your court proclaims you a descendant of the Prophet, and your Sufi followers revere you as their Perfect Guide, whose orders they disobey on pain of death; yet within living memory the tribal chiefs murdered a shah.
tiers.kid: The shah ruled Iran with total power and built a splendid new capital at Isfahan.
tiers.rise: Only a prince of the Safavid house could reign. In the 16th century the Qizilbash chiefs had ruled for the ten-year-old Tahmasp I and assassinated Ismail II, and the shahs kept the princes of their own family confined to the harem.
tiers.why: The shah stood at the apex of the state with total power over it.

tiers.name: Qizilbash lords
tiers.you: You are an amir of the Shamlu, wearing the red cap of the Safavid order; your father governed a province like a petty shah, but now the shah moves governors at will, and ghulams are taking their places.
tiers.kid: The Qizilbash were warrior tribes in red caps who had helped the first Safavid shah win his throne.
tiers.rise: Rank came from the tribe and its leading clans, though the sons of nobles had to prove themselves worthy of their fathers’ posts. A tribesman who forsook his tribe for the shah alone could join the Shahsevans, the “Friends of the King”, 12,000 strong under Abbas.
tiers.why: The Qizilbash, “red heads” after their twelve-gored crimson caps, were mainly Turkoman tribes of Anatolia and Azerbaijan, sworn followers of the Safavid order, who had won the throne for Ismail I in 1501.

tiers.name: Persian officials
tiers.you: You keep the revenue accounts in Persian, as your father did before you; your post depends on your skill and on the shah’s favour, and a superintendent records every decision you make.
tiers.kid: Persian officials wrote the shah’s letters, kept his accounts and ran his government.
tiers.rise: Offices were given, in principle, for merit: sons of officials were considered for their fathers’ posts but had to prove themselves, and laymen are recorded rising to high office. From Tahmasp’s reign the sons of Turkic officers were educated in Persian in the royal household and began to take posts once kept for Persians.
tiers.why: Persians, the “men of the pen”, filled the bureaucracy as they had under earlier rulers of Iran, while the Turkic-speaking soldiers were the “men of the sword”.

tiers.name: The shah's slave soldiers and officers
tiers.you: You were carried off from Georgia, made a Muslim and trained as the shah’s slave; now you ride in his cavalry, and if he favours you, you may one day govern a province.
tiers.kid: Ghulams were soldiers from the Caucasus who served only the shah, and some became generals and governors.
tiers.rise: Men entered as captives or deportees and, after special training, joined the new regiments or the royal household; from there the most favoured rose to govern provinces and command armies.
tiers.why: The ghulams, “slaves of the shah”, were Georgians, Circassians and Armenians brought from the Caucasus as captives and deportees, converted to Islam and trained for his service.

tiers.name: Shi'i clergy and sayyids
tiers.you: You were trained in Shi’i law, judge your neighbours’ disputes as a qazi under the governor, and draw part of the income of lands that their owners gave to the clergy to keep them from confiscation.
tiers.kid: Shi’i Muslim scholars served as judges and were seen as protectors of ordinary people.
tiers.rise: Rank among the ulama came by learning and the shah’s grants; a seyyed’s standing came by descent from the Prophet. Gifts of vaqf land turned many clerical families into landowners, a new and significant group in the words of the chronicler Iskandar Munshi.
tiers.why: Ismail I made Twelver Shi’ism the state religion and conversion mandatory for a largely Sunni population; Sunni scholars were killed or exiled, and Twelver scholars were brought in and given land and money in return…

tiers.name: Merchants and guild craftsmen
tiers.you: You weave carpets in a Tabriz workshop for merchants who sell them to the English and Dutch, and your guild runs its own affairs under a kadkhoda your community chose.
tiers.kid: Persian craftspeople made famous carpets and silks that were sold as far away as England.
tiers.rise: Trade could make a fortune, but property was insecure, so many owners put their land in the clergy’s hands as vaqf. The alliance between the bazaar and the ulama became a lasting feature of Iranian society.
tiers.why: Merchants and craftsmen stood at the base of the hierarchy with the peasants, yet the bazaar was one of the three powers Abbas I gathered around Naqsh-e Jahan Square, beside the mosque and the palace.

tiers.name: Peasants and herders
tiers.you: You farm with your own oxen and labour and keep two-fifths of the harvest; the rest goes to the landlord who provides the land, water and seed, and you may still be called out for forced labour.
tiers.kid: Most people in Safavid Iran were farmers who grew fruit, melons and tobacco, or herders who raised animals.
tiers.rise: The shahs moved whole peoples onto the land: under Abbas some 130,000–200,000 Georgians, about 300,000 Armenians and tens of thousands of Circassians were brought into Iran, many of them settled as farmers and cattle breeders. Under Shah Safi, the people put under royal commissioners in place of governors suffered from their rapacity and corruption.
tiers.why: Pastoralism and agriculture were the twin bases of the economy, and the lower levels of society were divided like the upper: Turkoman tribes bred livestock and lived apart from their neighbours, while Persians farmed…

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You were carried off from Circassia in the shah’s wars into a harem, where cliques of Circassian, Georgian and Turkmen women vie for the shah’s attention, and some captives like you have become his wives.
tiers.kid: Many enslaved people were captives from the Caucasus mountains, made to serve in palaces and armies.
tiers.rise: People were enslaved by capture in war. Conversion and training could make a man a ghulam, and the shahs raised even queen mothers from the women of the harem.
tiers.why: Most of the enslaved were captives from the Caucasus.
